items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 7355: Scaling to Multimodal and Multichannel Heart Sound Classification with Synthetic and Augmented Biosignals
items.summary: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of death worldwide, accounting for approximately 17.9 million deaths each year. Effective treatment requires early detection, which can be achieved with accurate and inexpensive pre-screening. This study uses a wearable vest which records real-world phonocardiogram (PCG) data from several auscultation sites at once (mPCG), but the cohort is small and the recordings noisy. To improve classification performance despite this limited, noisy dataset, signal processing augmentation and the denoising diffusion models WaveGrad and DiffWave supply additional training data for fine-tuning a pre-trained Wav2Vec 2.0 encoder. This work evaluates augmentation across three settings with increasingly complex inputs and smaller recording datasets: single-channel PCG, synchronised PCG and electrocardiogram (ECG), and six-channel mPCG. Accuracy, unweighted average recall (UAR) and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) reach 92.98%, 92.48% and 0.8064 on the Computing in Cardiology (CinC) 2016 single-channel PCG dataset, 93.14%, 92.21% and 0.8380 on its synchronised PCG-ECG training-a subset, and 77.13%, 74.25% and 0.5082 on the vest mPCG dataset. On a separate 40-subject vest hold-out, the SVM achieves mean accuracy, UAR and MCC of 79.17%, 72.22% and 0.574, respectively. Ablations examine pre-training, augmentation, generated data and encoder adaptation. For the primary classification configurations, the combination of original, conventionally augmented and generated data gives the highest mean performance.

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 7340: Revealing Misclassification of Exercise Sessions in Wearable Stress Detection for Automated Insulin Delivery
items.summary: Psychological stress tends to raise blood glucose and moderate exercise to lower it, so automated insulin delivery in type 1 diabetes could use wrist-worn stress detection that does not mistake exercise for stress. The only public wristband dataset known to us that combines induced stress with structured exercise (36 participants) reports accuracies of 0.84-0.93, but its evaluation did not keep participants apart, and each class was recorded in a separate session. Under a pre-registered plan, we re-implemented the published evaluation and repeated it on held-out participants, tested whether elapsed time and motion alone separated the classes, and counted stress-detector alarms during exercise. Our re-implementation did not match all published accuracies, held-out evaluation lowered exercise-recognition balanced accuracy by 0.05, and elapsed time alone separated stress from rest above chance. A physiology-only stress detector flagged 96% of exercise-session windows, including 80% of seated windows before exercise began (post hoc). In exploratory analyses, a detector trained with exercise examples rarely flagged exercise within the dataset, although motion features alone did almost as well (post hoc), and it missed a social stress test in an external dataset. Stress detectors for insulin delivery need validation on independent recordings combining strong stress with exercise.

items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 7346: Personalized Expert Routing for Short-Term PPG-Based Stress Detection
items.summary: Stressis a psychological state that significantly impacts mental and cardiovascular health when prolonged, making continuous wearable monitoring valuable. Photoplethysmography (PPG) signals are especially practical, yet existing PPG-based stress-detection methods rely on long data segments (30 s or longer), whereas recent PPG-based research increasingly adopts 10 s windows. Moreover, strict subject-independent evaluation reveals substantial performance degradation due to inter-subject physiological variability, while stress labels are rarely available for new users. To address these challenges, this work proposes a short-term PPG stress detection framework. A backbone is first pre-trained on VitalDB, a large-scale clinical PPG dataset that carries no stress labels; we show that such stress-label-free pre-training-which short-term stress-detection methods have not exploited-still transfers to downstream stress detection. This backbone then feeds a Personalized Expert Routing (PER) module, which routes each sample to specialized expert networks. Routing is guided by two complementary signals-the user's resting-state PPG features and the current signal's content-so the model adapts to individual differences without new-user stress labels. Under subject-independent 5-fold cross-validation on WESAD, CATSA, and CLAS, the proposed method achieves an average F1-score of 0.6919, an average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.7521, and an average accuracy of 0.6883, outperforming the strongest baseline by 4.14, 4.67, and 3.12 percentage points, respectively.

items.title: Multimodal deep learning approach for frailty classification using electrocardiogram and chest X-ray imaging
items.summary: by JinYong Park, Jung-Yeon Choi, Kwang-il Kim Frailty is a critical age-related syndrome associated with increased risks of disability, hospitalization, and mortality. While Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA) is the standard for evaluation, it is often subjective, time-consuming, and resource-intensive. To address these limitations, this study developed and validated a multimodal deep learning framework that integrates chest X-rays (CXR) and electrocardiograms (ECG) to provide an objective and rapid tool for frailty classification. We retrospectively analyzed data from 2,830 older adults who underwent CGA between 2007 and 2024, partitioned chronologically into training, validation, and test sets. Frailty was defined using a Multidimensional Frailty Score (MFS) > 5. Three deep learning models were trained and evaluated: a CXR-only model (EVA-X vision transformer), an ECG-only model (DenseNet-121), and a multimodal model combining both inputs. The multimodal model outperformed the single-modality models and four non-imaging clinical baseline models incorporating age, sex, comorbidity index, or routine laboratory variables, achieving the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.778 and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) of 0.726. For continuous MFS estimation, the multimodal model achieved the highest Pearson correlation (r = 0.610) and the lowest mean absolute error (MAE = 1.68) among the evaluated models. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) was used to qualitatively explore the image regions that influenced model predictions. This multimodal AI framework demonstrates modest classification performance and feasibility for frailty screening. By leveraging routinely collected clinical images, this framework may serve as a practical screening adjunct to identify older adults who may benefit from formal CGA. items.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 7297: In Vitro Dynamic Characterization of a Continuous Glucose Monitoring System Using an Independently Measured Glucose Profile: Amplitude Transfer, Rate Transfer, and Consecutive-Day Agreement
items.summary: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) sensors are evaluated almost exclusively in clinical studies. We investigated the dynamic response of one factory-calibrated CGM system on a programmable in vitro flow platform, with glucose measured independently by a SUPER GL2 analyzer as comparator. Twelve sensors were studied: four during verification of the measurement procedure (Stage 1) and eight tested on two consecutive days (Stage 2) under a 90 270 90 mg/dL profile. Amplitude transfer (KA) and apparent rising- and falling-phase slope transfer (Kup, Kdown) were calculated without lag correction. Stage 1 results were exploratory owing to an unexplained CGM displacement of approximately 35 min. The delivered profile differed from the programmed one in every Stage 2 run (upper plateaus 254-268 vs. 270 mg/dL). Mean KA was 0.731 and 0.731, Kup 0.749 and 0.746, and Kdown 0.729 and 0.719 on the two days; between sensors, KA ranged from 0.61-0.84. Near-zero mean paired changes reflected opposite group shifts (KA +0.026 and -0.025). Descriptive ICC(A,1) values of 0.919-0.952 (seven or eight pairs from two shared runs) indicate preserved between-sensor differences rather than established reproducibility. Bias ( -50 mg/dL) and MARD (31-32%) apply only to these in vitro conditions; the findings do not establish clinical performance or long-term stability.

items.title: Passive Monitoring for Detecting Hypomanic Symptoms in Bipolar Disorder Using Explainable Machine Learning: Longitudinal Observational Study
items.summary: Background: When trying to intervene early to prevent manic episodes, clinicians are hindered by patients underreporting their symptoms as they are becoming hypomanic or manic (ie, emerging symptoms). Continuous passive monitoring using wearable technology offers a potential solution to address this problem by capturing behavioral signals that do not depend on self-awareness. However, its clinical usefulness requires validation before implementation. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate whether passively collected wearable data can detect hypomanic symptoms using an explainable machine learning framework. Methods: We applied explainable machine learning to densely sampled multimodal data from a 2-year observational study of digital monitoring in 178 patients with a diagnosis of bipolar disorder (mean follow-up 540 days; range 120-706 days). Data on activity and sleep were collected continuously using wearable technology. Self-reported data were collected daily on their mood, energy, and anxiety, and weekly using the Altman Self-Rating Mania Scale (ASRM). To identify robust digital markers of hypomanic symptoms, we analyzed 252 time- and frequency-domain features from 43 participants who experienced at least 1 ASRM-defined symptomatic interval. Results: Passively collected data achieved high accuracy, comparable with daily self-reported data in detecting symptomatic intervals (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.91 vs 0.93, respectively). Combined daily passive wearable data features achieved higher sensitivity (92.0% vs 85.4%), balanced accuracy (0.90 vs 0.89), and stronger rule-out usefulness (negative predictive value 97.8% vs 96.1%) than self-report data, with daily sleep features alone driving most of this signal (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.91, sensitivity 91.8%). items.title: Sensor-wide association studies: a methodological architecture for developing and evaluating functional human traits
items.summary: BackgroundWearable and other digital sensors enable longitudinal observation of physiology and behaviour. However, reproducible associations and predictive performance do not establish which physiological construct a sensor-derived representation measures. An explicit framework is needed to distinguish statistical representation, construct interpretation and mechanistic explanation.ObjectiveThis Hypothesis and Theory article proposes Functional Human Traits (FHTs) and Sensor-Wide Association Studies (SWAS) as a conceptual and methodological architecture for developing and evaluating individual-level representations of physiological response capacities.Conceptual frameworkAn FHT is defined as a quantitative representation of a specified physiological response capacity, supported by temporal repeatability over a justified interval and independent biological evidence under stated conditions. SWAS links documented sensor features, exploratory analysis, candidate construction and independent evaluation. Outcome-guided screening estimates feature–outcome associations, whereas unsupervised analysis identifies statistical structure; neither directly identifies a physiological construct. Candidate construction requires an explicit measurement model, individual-level estimation with uncertainty and tests addressing competing interpretations. Evaluation distinguishes statistical replication, technical robustness, temporal repeatability and biological support. A hypothetical cardiovascular heat-response example illustrates candidate construction using a longitudinal model. Environmental sensing and semantic integration are optional supporting components where relevant to the research question.ImplicationsSWAS integrates established association-study and sensor-based measurement principles around explicit FHT identification requirements. items.title: [Viewpoint] Wear time matters: optimising wearables for clinically aligned and personalised health monitoring
items.summary: Wearable devices hold transformative potential for healthcare, yet their clinical impact is undermined by suboptimal long-term adherence. Although 24/7 always-on monitoring remains the default for maximising data completeness, achieving sustained wear could be limited by discomfort, inconvenience, or perceived lack of relevance, particularly during longitudinal monitoring. The clinical utility of wearables also depends on intelligent systems that filter, contextualise, and prioritise the resulting data into timely and actionable insights for individuals and clinicians.

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 7355: Scaling to Multimodal and Multichannel Heart Sound Classification with Synthetic and Augmented Biosignals
academic.summary: Cardiovascular diseases (CVDs) are the leading cause of death worldwide, accounting for approximately 17.9 million deaths each year. Effective treatment requires early detection, which can be achieved with accurate and inexpensive pre-screening. This study uses a wearable vest which records real-world phonocardiogram (PCG) data from several auscultation sites at once (mPCG), but the cohort is small and the recordings noisy. To improve classification performance despite this limited, noisy dataset, signal processing augmentation and the denoising diffusion models WaveGrad and DiffWave supply additional training data for fine-tuning a pre-trained Wav2Vec 2.0 encoder. This work evaluates augmentation across three settings with increasingly complex inputs and smaller recording datasets: single-channel PCG, synchronised PCG and electrocardiogram (ECG), and six-channel mPCG. Accuracy, unweighted average recall (UAR) and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) reach 92.98%, 92.48% and 0.8064 on the Computing in Cardiology (CinC) 2016 single-channel PCG dataset, 93.14%, 92.21% and 0.8380 on its synchronised PCG-ECG training-a subset, and 77.13%, 74.25% and 0.5082 on the vest mPCG dataset. On a separate 40-subject vest hold-out, the SVM achieves mean accuracy, UAR and MCC of 79.17%, 72.22% and 0.574, respectively. Ablations examine pre-training, augmentation, generated data and encoder adaptation. For the primary classification configurations, the combination of original, conventionally augmented and generated data gives the highest mean performance.

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 7340: Revealing Misclassification of Exercise Sessions in Wearable Stress Detection for Automated Insulin Delivery
academic.summary: Psychological stress tends to raise blood glucose and moderate exercise to lower it, so automated insulin delivery in type 1 diabetes could use wrist-worn stress detection that does not mistake exercise for stress. The only public wristband dataset known to us that combines induced stress with structured exercise (36 participants) reports accuracies of 0.84-0.93, but its evaluation did not keep participants apart, and each class was recorded in a separate session. Under a pre-registered plan, we re-implemented the published evaluation and repeated it on held-out participants, tested whether elapsed time and motion alone separated the classes, and counted stress-detector alarms during exercise. Our re-implementation did not match all published accuracies, held-out evaluation lowered exercise-recognition balanced accuracy by 0.05, and elapsed time alone separated stress from rest above chance. A physiology-only stress detector flagged 96% of exercise-session windows, including 80% of seated windows before exercise began (post hoc). In exploratory analyses, a detector trained with exercise examples rarely flagged exercise within the dataset, although motion features alone did almost as well (post hoc), and it missed a social stress test in an external dataset. Stress detectors for insulin delivery need validation on independent recordings combining strong stress with exercise.

academic.title: Sensors, Vol. 26, Pages 7346: Personalized Expert Routing for Short-Term PPG-Based Stress Detection
academic.summary: Stressis a psychological state that significantly impacts mental and cardiovascular health when prolonged, making continuous wearable monitoring valuable. Photoplethysmography (PPG) signals are especially practical, yet existing PPG-based stress-detection methods rely on long data segments (30 s or longer), whereas recent PPG-based research increasingly adopts 10 s windows. Moreover, strict subject-independent evaluation reveals substantial performance degradation due to inter-subject physiological variability, while stress labels are rarely available for new users. To address these challenges, this work proposes a short-term PPG stress detection framework. A backbone is first pre-trained on VitalDB, a large-scale clinical PPG dataset that carries no stress labels; we show that such stress-label-free pre-training-which short-term stress-detection methods have not exploited-still transfers to downstream stress detection. This backbone then feeds a Personalized Expert Routing (PER) module, which routes each sample to specialized expert networks. Routing is guided by two complementary signals-the user's resting-state PPG features and the current signal's content-so the model adapts to individual differences without new-user stress labels. Under subject-independent 5-fold cross-validation on WESAD, CATSA, and CLAS, the proposed method achieves an average F1-score of 0.6919, an average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.7521, and an average accuracy of 0.6883, outperforming the strongest baseline by 4.14, 4.67, and 3.12 percentage points, respectively.

academic.title: Multimodal deep learning approach for frailty classification using electrocardiogram and chest X-ray imaging
academic.summary: by JinYong Park, Jung-Yeon Choi, Kwang-il Kim Frailty is a critical age-related syndrome associated with increased risks of disability, hospitalization, and mortality. While Comprehensive Geriatric Assessment (CGA) is the standard for evaluation, it is often subjective, time-consuming, and resource-intensive. To address these limitations, this study developed and validated a multimodal deep learning framework that integrates chest X-rays (CXR) and electrocardiograms (ECG) to provide an objective and rapid tool for frailty classification. We retrospectively analyzed data from 2,830 older adults who underwent CGA between 2007 and 2024, partitioned chronologically into training, validation, and test sets. Frailty was defined using a Multidimensional Frailty Score (MFS) > 5. Three deep learning models were trained and evaluated: a CXR-only model (EVA-X vision transformer), an ECG-only model (DenseNet-121), and a multimodal model combining both inputs. The multimodal model outperformed the single-modality models and four non-imaging clinical baseline models incorporating age, sex, comorbidity index, or routine laboratory variables, achieving the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.778 and area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) of 0.726. For continuous MFS estimation, the multimodal model achieved the highest Pearson correlation (r = 0.610) and the lowest mean absolute error (MAE = 1.68) among the evaluated models. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) was used to qualitatively explore the image regions that influenced model predictions. This multimodal AI framework demonstrates modest classification performance and feasibility for frailty screening. By leveraging routinely collected clinical images, this framework may serve as a practical screening adjunct to identify older adults who may benefit from formal CGA. academic.summary: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) sensors are evaluated almost exclusively in clinical studies. We investigated the dynamic response of one factory-calibrated CGM system on a programmable in vitro flow platform, with glucose measured independently by a SUPER GL2 analyzer as comparator. Twelve sensors were studied: four during verification of the measurement procedure (Stage 1) and eight tested on two consecutive days (Stage 2) under a 90 270 90 mg/dL profile. Amplitude transfer (KA) and apparent rising- and falling-phase slope transfer (Kup, Kdown) were calculated without lag correction. Stage 1 results were exploratory owing to an unexplained CGM displacement of approximately 35 min. The delivered profile differed from the programmed one in every Stage 2 run (upper plateaus 254-268 vs. 270 mg/dL). Mean KA was 0.731 and 0.731, Kup 0.749 and 0.746, and Kdown 0.729 and 0.719 on the two days; between sensors, KA ranged from 0.61-0.84. Near-zero mean paired changes reflected opposite group shifts (KA +0.026 and -0.025). Descriptive ICC(A,1) values of 0.919-0.952 (seven or eight pairs from two shared runs) indicate preserved between-sensor differences rather than established reproducibility. Bias ( -50 mg/dL) and MARD (31-32%) apply only to these in vitro conditions; the findings do not establish clinical performance or long-term stability.

academic.summary: Background: When trying to intervene early to prevent manic episodes, clinicians are hindered by patients underreporting their symptoms as they are becoming hypomanic or manic (ie, emerging symptoms). Continuous passive monitoring using wearable technology offers a potential solution to address this problem by capturing behavioral signals that do not depend on self-awareness. However, its clinical usefulness requires validation before implementation. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate whether passively collected wearable data can detect hypomanic symptoms using an explainable machine learning framework. Methods: We applied explainable machine learning to densely sampled multimodal data from a 2-year observational study of digital monitoring in 178 patients with a diagnosis of bipolar disorder (mean follow-up 540 days; range 120-706 days). academic.title: Sensor-wide association studies: a methodological architecture for developing and evaluating functional human traits
academic.summary: BackgroundWearable and other digital sensors enable longitudinal observation of physiology and behaviour. However, reproducible associations and predictive performance do not establish which physiological construct a sensor-derived representation measures. An explicit framework is needed to distinguish statistical representation, construct interpretation and mechanistic explanation.ObjectiveThis Hypothesis and Theory article proposes Functional Human Traits (FHTs) and Sensor-Wide Association Studies (SWAS) as a conceptual and methodological architecture for developing and evaluating individual-level representations of physiological response capacities.Conceptual frameworkAn FHT is defined as a quantitative representation of a specified physiological response capacity, supported by temporal repeatability over a justified interval and independent biological evidence under stated conditions. SWAS links documented sensor features, exploratory analysis, candidate construction and independent evaluation. Outcome-guided screening estimates feature–outcome associations, whereas unsupervised analysis identifies statistical structure; neither directly identifies a physiological construct. Candidate construction requires an explicit measurement model, individual-level estimation with uncertainty and tests addressing competing interpretations. Evaluation distinguishes statistical replication, technical robustness, temporal repeatability and biological support. A hypothetical cardiovascular heat-response example illustrates candidate construction using a longitudinal model. Environmental sensing and semantic integration are optional supporting components where relevant to the research question.ImplicationsSWAS integrates established association-study and sensor-based measurement principles around explicit FHT identification requirements. academic.title: [Viewpoint] Wear time matters: optimising wearables for clinically aligned and personalised health monitoring
academic.summary: Wearable devices hold transformative potential for healthcare, yet their clinical impact is undermined by suboptimal long-term adherence. Although 24/7 always-on monitoring remains the default for maximising data completeness, achieving sustained wear could be limited by discomfort, inconvenience, or perceived lack of relevance, particularly during longitudinal monitoring. The clinical utility of wearables also depends on intelligent systems that filter, contextualise, and prioritise the resulting data into timely and actionable insights for individuals and clinicians.

scarcityTaxonomy.note: Top Signals selection rubric. Each Top Signals item MUST be labeled with exactly one category from `categories`, assigned a frequency anchor (`annual`/`quarterly`/`monthly`), and scored as `base_score × anchor_weight`. LLM only does category+anchor matching — it does NOT need historical knowledge (categories define scarcity, not LLM memory). Revise quarterly based on dogfooding.

anchor_definitions.annual: Once-a-year or rarer event within this category (e.g., FDA's first consumer-grade AFib clearance for a wearable — happens at most once a year globally).
anchor_definitions.quarterly: Few-per-year event within this category (e.g., a major vendor's new regulatory clearance in a new jurisdiction).
anchor_definitions.monthly: Routine-but-still-notable within this category (e.g., another vendor achieving a similar clearance that's already established).

categories.criteria: FDA 510(k) / De Novo / PMA, CE mark MDR, NMPA certification, PMDA, TGA — for a wearable health feature. Peer-reviewed multi-site prospective clinical validation also qualifies.
examples_positive: Apple Watch gets FDA clearance for new sleep apnea detection
Samsung Health Monitor BP approved in US
Oura ring NMPA class-II certification
examples_negative: Another vendor clones an already-approved feature in a new region (→ monthly anchor, not annual)

categories.criteria: Company or academic publicly releases model weights, pretrained foundation model, large labeled dataset, or production-grade SDK/code for wearable/physiological signals. Must be usable (not just a paper claiming 'code coming soon').
examples_positive: Meta releases wearable foundation model weights on HuggingFace
Stanford/Apple release 1M-ECG labeled dataset
Google open-sources Fitbit sleep staging model
examples_negative: Academic paper promises code release but repo is empty

categories.criteria: M&A, major exec/founder departure or appointment at a wearable company, large funding round (≥$50M), strategic pivot announcement. Affects competitive landscape or talent flow.
examples_positive: Google acquires Oura
Shwetak Patel leaves Google Health for X startup
WHOOP pivots from consumer to B2B-clinical

categories.criteria: Consumer wearable first-time integration of a physical/biochemical sensing modality (non-invasive BP, non-invasive glucose, EMG, sweat cortisol, SpHb, real-time hydration, etc.). Must ship in a real product, not just a research paper.
examples_positive: Samsung ships first consumer non-invasive glucose on Galaxy Watch
Apple adds wrist-based cuffless BP to Series X
Oura integrates continuous sweat-lactate sensor
examples_negative: New optical HR sensor iteration in existing form factor (already-done modality)
Academic prototype for a new sensor — belongs in algorithmic_breakthrough or open_release if qualifying

categories.criteria: New SOTA with concrete metric on wearable/physiological task, OR foundation-model / self-supervised training at ≥10M-sample scale, OR on-device breakthrough with specific latency/size/power numbers. Must have reproducible evidence (paper with code, benchmark result).
examples_positive: ECG foundation model at 11M samples with systematic SSL comparison (example)
On-device AFib detection at <5ms/inference on Apple S10 chip
New sleep-stage SOTA on SHHS with 3pp gain
examples_negative: Incremental +1pp gain with cherry-picked test set

categories.criteria: Prospective or multi-site clinical study with n≥10,000 participants OR multi-center design, wearable-derived endpoint, peer-reviewed or at top conference.
examples_positive: Ultrahuman Ring N=3086 longitudinal sleep study (today's example — note: n<10k but near-threshold + longitudinal design keeps it in this category at monthly anchor)
All of Us cohort wearable analysis n>50k
Apple Heart Study n=419k

categories.criteria: Wearable vendor first-time entry into new go-to-market category: clinical services, B2B/B2B2C, insurance, subscription, EHR integration, pharma partnership. Must be a real product launch, not a trial balloon.
examples_positive: WHOOP launches clinician video visits + HealthEx EHR integration (today's example)
Oura partners with large insurer for reimbursed rings
Apple Watch Atrial Fibrillation History gets CMS reimbursement code
examples_negative: New subscription tier of existing product

categories.criteria: HealthKit / Health Connect / Samsung Health SDK / Huawei Health Kit / Wear OS schema, new data type, permission, or interoperability standard (FHIR wearables profile). Must be shipping, not WWDC keynote hype.
examples_positive: HealthKit adds glucose trend data type in watchOS 27
Health Connect adds cross-app mental-health schema
New IEEE standard for wearable data exchange ratified
